title: 38. The effects of increasing concentrations of altrenogest on primary satellite cells.
content:
Abstract
Altrenogest (ALT) is a synthetic progesterone analogue utilized in the equine industry as an estrus suppressant to mitigate the negative behaviors of performance horses. With a structural similarity to anabolic steroids such as trenbolone acetate, there are concerns that administration of ALT could be enhancing the skeletal muscle hypertrophy potential of performance horses. The International Equestrian Federation prohibits its use in stallions and geldings and highly regulates its use in mares due to concerns over its anabolic potential. Satellite cells are the primary driver for postnatal skeletal muscle hypertrophy in mammals. Understanding the effects of ALT on satellite cell activity is critical to knowing if this widely used practice is granting an advantage to performance horses by increasing their skeletal muscle hypertrophy potential. Data was collected using ovine satellite cells (OSC) as a model. The primary objective is optimization of ALT treatment concentrations and examining their effects on OSC proliferation and protein synthesis rates. Primary OSC were isolated from the hindlimb of 9-month old commercial hair sheep wethers (n = 3). Proliferation analysis was performed with OSC cultures grown to approximately 70% confluency, followed by treatment with 5% fetal bovine serum (FBS) or increasing concentrations of ALT at 7.5 nM, 8.5 nM, 10 nM or 30 nM in 5% FBS. Proliferation rates were measured 24-h post treatment. Protein synthesis OSC cultures were grown to approximately 80% confluency and induced to differentiate. 48-h later, cultures were treated with serum free media (SFM) or ALT at 10 nM or 30 nM in SFM. Protein synthesis rates were measured 6-h post-treatment. Increasing dosages of ALT did not linearly (p = 0.37) or quadratically (p = 0.25) impact proliferation rates of primary OSC. Similarly, initial data indicates that protein synthesis rates of fused OSC were not linearly (p = 0.37) or quadratically (p = 0.76) impacted by ALT. These findings suggest that ALT does not impact proliferation rates of primary OSC or protein synthesis rates of fused OSC. However, future work is warranted to evaluate the effects of ALT in equine satellite cells and elucidate potential roles that ALT plays in equine skeletal muscle biology.
